study_type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical studies
key_claims: Prescription medications such as metformin, semaglutide, and anti-TNF therapies were associated with the strongest reductions in biological age markers.
Combining regular physical activity with healthy eating plans, including Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets, consistently reduced epigenetic age.
Over-the-counter supplements and certain medical procedures evaluated in the research generally failed to show measurable reductions in biological age.
Newer epigenetic clocks proved more sensitive and responsive to anti-aging interventions than older clock versions.
limitations: It remains unproven whether reducing biological age markers leads to extended lifespan or a lower risk of age-related diseases.
Researchers have not yet determined if biological age changes are directly caused by the treatments or by unaccounted external factors.
The duration of biological age changes, how quickly they occur, and the exact underlying biological mechanisms are still unknown.
what_not_to_say: Do not claim that taking metformin, semaglutide, or anti-TNF drugs guarantees a longer life or prevents chronic diseases.
Do not state that over-the-counter supplements are universally harmful or completely devoid of any general health benefits.
Do not present reductions in DNA methylation age as definitive proof of reversed clinical aging.
